intro: The finale of La Mer begins with low strings churning beneath timpani and bass drum. Calls from the first movement return, and a brass chorale crowns the last rush towards D♭ major.

sections.label: A · Low strings and a trumpet call
sections.mNote: Restless low strings surround the muted trumpet’s phrase

sections.label: B · Wind phrases over running strings
sections.mNote: Long wind phrases stretch above the quick accompaniment

sections.label: C · Flutes, harps and quiet strings
sections.mNote: Wind solos and harp figures emerge between the larger exchanges

sections.label: D · Brass above the moving strings
sections.mNote: Horns and trumpets enlarge the phrases

sections.label: Coda · The chorale and final rush
sections.mNote: The brass chorale returns before the D♭-major ending

cues.title: The storm starts low
cues.text: Animé et tumultueux — animated and tumultuous. Timpani and bass drum rumble softly while cellos and basses climb in short, twisting figures. The tam-tam adds a dark ring. Most of the orchestra is still silent.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, movement III, printed p. 223: timpani, bass drum, tam-tam and low-string figures. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/b/b6/IMSLP15420-Debussy_-_La_Mer_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A muted trumpet calls
cues.text: A muted trumpet sounds above the low strings, beside oboe and clarinet phrases. For part of this passage the double basses bow close to the bridge, giving their held notes a thin, grainy edge.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, rehearsal 43, printed p. 224: trumpet marked Sourdines; divided basses marked Sur le chevalet.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Lalo misses the sea
cues.text: Reviewing the 1905 première in Le Temps, Pierre Lalo writes: “I do not hear, I do not see, I do not smell the sea.” Debussy’s new score has disappointed one of his former admirers.
cues.evidence: Pierre Lalo, Le Temps, review following the Paris première of 15 October 1905, quoted in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_mer_(Debussy), Reception. Debussy’s reply is discussed at https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer.

cues.title: A tune over triplets
cues.text: The longer wind phrases stretch over much quicker string figures. Groups of two and three cross beneath them. Debussy can make a melody seem to float while the accompaniment is working furiously.
cues.evidence: Jacob Greenberg describes the finale’s superimposed duplets and triplets and sustained wind theme: https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer. Durand full score, movement III.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: The dawn calls back
cues.text: The first movement’s trumpet call belongs to this finale too. Debussy brings back its shape among the stormier exchanges, and later restores the broad chorale. The music of dawn has survived into a rougher sea.
cues.evidence: Susan Key discusses the finale’s returns from movement I: https://www.laphil.com/works/la-mer. Durand full score, movements I and III; this is a movement-wide relationship.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Flutes above two harps
cues.text: In the quieter middle pages, flutes and oboes share little phrases above the two harps. The horns hold long notes, and the first violins sustain high above the moving inner strings. There is suddenly room around each line.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, printed pp. 250–252: wind phrases, two moving harp parts, sustained horns and first violins.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Debussy conducts his sea
cues.text: In January 1908 Debussy stands before the Paris orchestra to conduct La Mer himself. The work that met such resistance in 1905 now brings him his greatest public success since Pelléas et Mélisande.
cues.evidence: Jacob Greenberg’s Boston Symphony programme note, on Debussy’s Paris performances of 19 and 26 January 1908: https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer

cues.title: The chorale returns
cues.text: The closing pages recover the first movement’s brass chorale. Horns and trombones hold the broad line against repeated wind notes and short string figures. Then Très animé sends the orchestra into its final rush.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, printed pp. 270–274, the chorale and rehearsal 61, Très animé. The established coda boundary locates this closing span.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One last plucked blow
cues.text: The final D♭-major chords have a sharp edge. After the orchestra’s last sustained blast, timpani strike once more with plucked strings. Debussy marks the attack sec — dry.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, final page, printed p. 279: final timpani and pizzicato string attack marked sec. Jacob Greenberg describes the same ending: https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The harps come through
transitions.from: B · Wind phrases over running strings
transitions.to: C · Flutes, harps and quiet strings
transitions.how: The brass exchanges subside into a passage for quieter winds and strings. Flutes and oboes share the tune above the two harps, while horns and double basses hold long notes. The first violins sustain high above the quicker viola and cello figures.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, printed pp. 248–252, the retreat and ensuing harp-and-wind passage.

transitions.title: The chorale crowns the sea
transitions.from: D · Brass above the moving strings
transitions.to: Coda · The chorale and final rush
transitions.how: The harmony turns towards D♭ major as the closing brass chorale emerges. Its broad notes stand over short, repeated string figures and a low brass foundation. The crescendo leads to Très animé, where the strings break into continuous running notes for the last rush.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, printed pp. 270–274: return to the five-flat signature, brass chorale and rehearsal 61, Très animé.

source.title: Debussy, La Mer · Durand full score, plates D. & F. 6532 / 6838
source.locator: Movement III, printed pp. 223–279: low strings and percussion at Animé et tumultueux, muted trumpet at rehearsal 43, the late brass chorale and Très animé at rehearsal 61.

timeline.note: Timpani, bass drum and tam-tam sound beneath the restless low strings.
Muted trumpet and woodwinds cut across the low strings; the basses play close to the bridge.
The wind phrases stretch across the running string figures.
Flutes and oboes sing above the two harps, with held horns and high violin notes.
Brass joins the wind phrases while the strings keep their quick accompaniment moving.
Short wind calls pass over quick string figures as the orchestra gathers for the closing chorale.
Winds, brass and strings drive through the final D♭-major chords; timpani and plucked strings give the last dry stroke.

composer.epithet: He trusted his ear over the rules — “pleasure is the law” — and made the piano, the flute and the orchestra sound new.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and went to prison for it, and there he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

His teachers could not make him out. Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, found “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament” in January 1874; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Years later, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud around 1890, he put his position plainly: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
